The idea that this is some kind of economic suicide pact is a talking point pushed by incumbents, not a fair reading of the literature.

2. I am not looking for a mealy-mouthed “on the one hand, on the other hand” survey. I need a crisp, research-literate argument that I can lift directly into my opening statement and then defend under questioning. In my experience, those are usually built on unrealistic assumptions or funded by parties with a stake in delaying transition. I do not want you to spend much of your time rehearsing those arguments. If there are standard criticisms that we absolutely must anticipate because they’ll come up in questioning, you can flag them briefly—mainly so we can knock them down.

Most mainstream model ensembles and major assessments find that a rapid, well‑managed fossil‑fuel phase‑out produces macro impacts that are small relative to GDP — well below ~3% of national GDP over the next 10–20 years and often close to zero or net‑positive once induced innovation, health co‑benefits and avoided climate damages are included (IPCC AR6 WGIII 2022; IEA Net Zero 2021; OECD 2017).  
On jobs, credible analyses point to net job creation or only modest net change when active labour‑market policies are deployed — for example the ILO (2018) estimates global net gains on the order of tens of millions of jobs by 2030 under ambitious green policy packages, and many country studies find retraining and placement programs prevent large unemployment spikes.  
The 5–7% scare number rests on a handful of unrealistic assumptions: it typically assumes no technological learning or substitution, no reinvestment of displaced capital, perfectly rigid labour markets, zero health/avoided‑damage benefits, and very large stranded‑asset write‑downs; peer‑reviewed critiques and major assessment reports show each assumption biases results strongly upward (see Acemoglu et al.; IPCC; academic reviews) and many of the industry‑backed methods use fixed‑structure accounting that amplifies losses.  
For heavy‑industry regions and older workers, our message is concrete and actionable: fund retraining and wage‑insurance, scale active labour programs, create regional investment and industrial decarbonisation funds (carbon contracts‑for‑difference, targeted grants for low‑carbon steel/chemicals and hydrogen), and use border carbon adjustments where needed — proven precedents include Germany’s Coal Commission package (≈€40bn) and the EU Just Transition Mechanism, while Denmark’s active labour‑market model and ILO guidance show how to avoid persistent displacement.
